Overall tone is mixed-to-slightly negative. The statement notes improving activity and robust job gains, but emphasizes elevated inflation driven by supply shocks (energy and supply-chain disruptions) and geopolitics. The policy response—raising the federal funds rate to 1.50–1.75% and commencing balance-sheet reduction—aligns with evidence that credible, forward-looking tightening helps anchor inflation expectations under inflation targeting (Svensson and Woodford, 2005) and with lessons from the Volcker disinflation about the value of strong commitment, even at some near-term growth cost. New Keynesian Phillips Curve insights (e.g., Galí) imply that adverse supply shocks (oil, logistics) raise inflation while weighing on output, consistent with the text’s cautious tone; VAR evidence on energy price shocks similarly shows growth headwinds from oil spikes. Recent “inflation-at-risk” work indicates a fattened right tail of inflation outcomes post-pandemic, justifying the Committee’s vigilance. Pandemic-era shifts in consumption baskets (e.g., Israel’s CPI weighting adjustments) underscore measurement uncertainty, reinforcing the case for a hawkish stance. Implementation specifics (IORB, ON RRP) reflect modern operating-framework principles discussed by Goodfriend (2002), improving rate control and policy transmission. Net effect: slightly negative sentiment, tempered by credible anti-inflation resolve.
